The neonatal body mass at this stage has been recorded at 7.0 grams [Wwb = 7.0 grams], derived from morphometric relationships established for this species. In the laboratory, fertilised ova require a period of about 137 days [ab = about 137 days] before the young begin active feeding, when maintained at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This incubation duration is relatively protracted compared to some other rajiforms, likely due to the cooler, thermally stable waters of the northeast Atlantic where this skate occurs. The onset of independent foraging marks a critical transition from reliance on endogenous yolk to exogenous prey capture, typically involving small benthic crustaceans. Juveniles grow steadily during their first year, adding both disc width and body mass while remaining vulnerable to predation by larger elasmobranchs. The relatively small birth size compared to adult dimensions underscores the substantial scope for somatic growth that characterises the life history of this species.

Growth in Cuckoo ray proceeds along a trajectory that culminates in an ultimate total length of 80 cm [Li = 80 cm], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 3326 grams [Wwi = approximately 3326 grams] in large, reproductively active individuals. These maxima are rarely observed in routine trawl surveys, as most captured specimens fall below these upper bounds, suggesting that full asymptotic size is achieved only by the oldest members of the population. Field records indicate that the total length at which gonadal maturation begins is 57 cm [Lp = 57 cm], a threshold at which individuals transition from the juvenile to the sub-adult stage. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 1161 grams [Wwp = approximately 1161 grams], reflecting the considerable accumulation of somatic tissue required before reproductive investment can commence. Sexual maturation in this species involves testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian maturation in females, both of which are size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent processes. The attainment of 57 cm total length typically coincides with a phase of accelerated growth, after which energy is increasingly directed toward gamete production rather than further increases in body dimensions.

The reproductive strategy of Leucoraja naevus is characterised by a low fecundity but continuous egg-laying schedule. Females deposit one to three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to three eggs per clutch], and under optimal conditions they may produce roughly two clutches each year [F_R_i = roughly two clutches each year]. This annual reproductive output is somewhat constrained by the large size of the individual egg cases, which require substantial maternal investment in yolk and protective capsule material. The maximum daily reproduction rate, estimated under stable captive conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], corresponds to 90 eggs over a full year [Ri = 90 eggs over a full year], a figure that integrates both clutch size and the interval between successive oviposition events. The timing of egg deposition is not strictly seasonal, and gravid individuals have been captured throughout the year in regions where bottom temperatures remain relatively constant. Sperm storage in the reproductive tract allows females to continue producing fertile clutches for several months after a single copulation event, which may buffer against low encounter rates with males in low-density populations.

Longevity is a key demographic parameter for stock assessment, as it dictates the number of reproductive years available to each female over her lifetime. The extended juvenile phase and late maturation make the species particularly sensitive to fishing mortality, since individuals may be captured and removed from the population well before they have contributed offspring to the next generation.

Comparative analyses within the Rajidae family highlight the intermediate position of Leucoraja naevus in terms of body size and reproductive output. Smaller skates such as the thorny skate reach puberty at a shorter total length, while larger species like the barndoor skate exceed 80 cm total length and produce a correspondingly higher fecundity. The life span of 14 years [am = 14 years] places the Cuckoo ray among the shorter-lived members of its genus, although direct comparisons are complicated by differences in water temperature across geographic ranges at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The age at birth of approximately 137 days [ab = approximately 137 days] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] is typical for oviparous skates, whose leathery egg cases provide physical protection during the lengthy incubation. The neonatal body mass of 7.0 grams [Wwb = 7.0 grams] and birth length of 11 cm [Lb = 11 cm] are consistent with allometric predictions based on adult body dimensions. Available data suggest that the species maintains a relatively constant growth rate during its juvenile years, with the transition to puberty occurring when approximately 70 percent of the ultimate length has been attained. Future studies focusing on the influence of temperature variation on embryonic development and juvenile growth would refine these demographic estimates.
